nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

questions.q: A large enterprise needs to enforce that all Azure resources must be deployed only in specific regions (West Europe and North Europe) across 80 subscriptions. New subscriptions added in the future must automatically comply. What is the MOST scalable approach?
choices: Create a custom RBAC role in each subscription that restricts deployment to those regions
Use Azure Blueprints to deploy resource locks in each subscription denying deployments outside the target regions
Enable Azure Defender and configure geo-restriction alerts for deployments in non-approved regions
Configure Azure Policy 'Allowed locations' initiative at the Management Group level and assign it to the root management
questions.explanation: Azure Policy assigned at a Management Group scope applies to ALL subscriptions within that group hierarchy, including subscriptions added in the future. The built-in 'Allowed locations' policy definition (or an initiative containing it) enforces the region constraint at creation time with a Deny effect. RBAC cannot restrict deployment regions. Blueprints are a deployment mechanism, not a continuous enforcement control. Azure Defender is a threat detection service. it automatically applies to all current and future subscriptions underneath

questions.q: A solutions architect must design an identity solution for a company with 10,000 on-premises Active Directory users who need SSO access to Azure resources and Microsoft 365. The company cannot allow password hashes to be stored in the cloud for compliance reasons. Which hybrid identity method satisfies this requirement?
choices: Password Hash Synchronization (PHS) — synchronize password hashes from on-premises AD to Azure AD for cloud authentication
Pass-Through Authentication (PTA) — install lightweight agents on-premises that validate passwords against AD without storing hashes in the cloud
ADFS federation via Azure AD Connect — authentication happens on-premises through ADFS servers; Azure AD acts only as a relying party
Azure AD B2C with custom policies and a SAML federation back to the on-premises directory for hybrid identity
questions.explanation: Pass-Through Authentication (PTA) validates users' passwords directly against on-premises Active Directory. No password hashes or tokens are stored in Azure AD — the authentication agent on-premises handles validation and returns a success/fail response. This satisfies compliance requirements that prohibit cloud storage of password hashes. ADFS federation also works but requires significant on-premises infrastructure. PHS explicitly stores password hashes in Azure AD, violating the requirement.

questions.q: An architect needs to grant a team of junior developers access to create and manage resources within a specific resource group, but prevent them from modifying any IAM/RBAC assignments. Which RBAC role combination achieves least-privilege?
choices: Assign the Owner role at the resource group scope, granting the team full resource management including modifying RBAC assignments and IAM permissions — exceeds least-privilege

Assign the Reader role plus a custom role with write permissions to create and manage specific resource provider types within the resource group — the team gets granular access but requires custom role maintenance
Assign the Contributor role at the resource group scope so the team can create and manage resources without modifying RBAC role assignments
Assign the User Access Administrator role scoped to the resource group, which grants the team rights to manage RBAC assignments but no ability to create or manage Azure resources directly
questions.explanation: The built-in Contributor role provides full rights to create, delete, and manage resources but explicitly does NOT include Microsoft.Authorization/* actions (assigning/removing roles, creating policy assignments). This is the correct least-privilege choice: full resource management without IAM modification rights. Owner includes Microsoft.Authorization/* which allows granting access. User Access Administrator is specifically for managing role assignments, the opposite of what's needed.

questions.q: A company's operations team needs to collect OS-level performance metrics (custom memory counters, application logs) from 500 Azure VMs and on-premises servers into a central workspace for dashboards and alerts. Which Azure Monitor component collects this data?
choices: Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) deployed to the VMs and Arc-enabled on-premises servers, configured via Data Collection Rules to send OS-level metrics to Log Analytics
Application Insights SDK integrated at the OS level on on-premises servers for infrastructure performance counters — designed for application telemetry, not OS metrics
Azure Monitor Diagnostic Settings on each VM and on-premises server — routes platform and guest-OS logs to Log Analytics, but limited to Azure-native resource metrics by default
Azure Monitor Metrics Explorer querying pre-collected metrics from on-premises servers
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) is the modern unified agent replacing the legacy Log Analytics Agent (MMA) and Diagnostics Agent. It uses Data Collection Rules (DCRs) to define which data sources to collect (Windows Event Logs, Syslog, performance counters, custom text logs) and which workspace(s) to send data to. AMA works on Azure VMs, on-premises servers (via Azure Arc), and multi-cloud VMs. Platform metrics don't require an agent but cannot collect OS-level custom counters or application logs.

questions.q: An architect is designing a resource management strategy for a large organization with 3 business units, each with Dev/Test/Prod environments. They need separate billing, access isolation, and policy enforcement per environment. What structure best reflects this?
choices: One subscription for all environments with resource groups per business unit and environment — flat structure with no management group hierarchy
An Azure Tenant per business unit with cross-tenant subscriptions for shared services — complex management group overhead across tenant boundaries
One subscription per environment type (Dev subscription, Test subscription, Prod subscription) without management group nesting to group by business unit
A management group hierarchy: Root → Business Unit MGs → Environment MGs.
questions.explanation: AZ-305 best practice for enterprise-scale: Management Groups provide policy/RBAC inheritance hierarchy. Separate subscriptions per BU×Environment provide billing isolation (each subscription has its own cost view), resource quota isolation, and a strong blast radius boundary. Policies assigned at the Environment MG (e.g., no public IPs in Prod) cascade to all BU Prod subscriptions automatically. One subscription for all environments creates governance and billing challenges. Multiple tenants add identity complexity without proportional benefit. with one subscription per business unit × environment combination (9 subscriptions total), policies and RBAC assigned at MG level

questions.q: A company needs to provide developers with self-service access to pre-approved Azure environments (specific VM sizes, approved images, region restrictions) without granting them broad subscription permissions. Which Azure service supports this governance pattern?
choices: Azure Managed Applications published to an internal Service Catalog, allowing developers to self-deploy pre-approved environments from the catalog without needing IT involvement
Azure Policy with 'allowed VM SKU' definitions and a pre-approved image list applied to subscriptions — governs compliance without enabling self-service deployment of full pre-approved environments
Azure Blueprints assignments that deploy pre-approved environments without granting developers reusable Service Catalog access to self-serve
Azure Resource Manager templates published in a Git repo and deployed by a central operations team, without self-service access for developers
questions.explanation: Azure Managed Applications published to a Service Catalog allow operators to define pre-approved resource packages (VMs with specific SKUs, approved OS images, networking configurations) that developers can deploy from the Azure portal without seeing the underlying ARM templates or having broad RBAC permissions. The managed resource group is owned by the publisher, ensuring approved configurations. Blueprints are for subscription-level governance scaffolding, not per-developer self-service deployments.

questions.q: An architect needs to design a solution where no single person can approve their own access to sensitive resources. All privileged role activations must require approval from a second person and generate an audit log. Which Azure feature provides this?
choices: Azure AD Access Reviews scheduled monthly to detect and revoke unauthorized privileged role assignments after the fact
Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM) configured with eligible role assignments and an approval workflow before activation
Azure RBAC deny assignments scoped to each privileged role to block users from approving their own access requests
Azure AD Conditional Access policies with role-based assignment conditions and a sign-in risk approval flow
questions.explanation: PIM eligible assignments require users to activate the role (not permanently assigned) and can be configured to require multi-person approval before activation. The approver receives a notification, reviews the business justification, and approves or denies. All activation requests, approvals, and denials are logged in Azure AD audit logs. Access Reviews verify existing assignments but don't enforce real-time approval workflows for new activations.

questions.q: A company wants to receive proactive alerts when their Azure costs exceed $10,000 in a given month, and automatically suspend non-critical development VMs when spending reaches 90% of the budget. Which Azure feature enables both of these?
choices: Azure Monitor metric alerts on billing metrics with Logic App workflows for VM management
Azure Advisor cost recommendations with automated remediation enabled
Azure Cost Management + Billing budget with action groups
Azure Policy with cost-based deny effects that prevent new resource creation above budget
questions.explanation: Azure Cost Management budgets allow you to set monthly spending thresholds with alert thresholds at multiple percentages (e.g., 80% and 90% of budget). At 90%, an action group can trigger an Azure Automation Runbook or Logic App that stops the development VMs. Email alerts notify cost owners at any threshold. Azure Advisor provides recommendations but not automated enforcement. Azure Policy cannot enforce budget-based restrictions.

nodes.title: Route users across two regions

choices: Azure Front Door
Azure Load Balancer
Application Gateway
Network Security Group

nodes.explanation: Azure Front Door (and Traffic Manager) provide global, cross-region entry with health probes and failover. Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway are regional only, so they can't route between regions.

nodes.title: DNS: Key Ideas
nodes.content: DNS turns names into addresses. Most outages traced to 'is it DNS?' get answered 'yes'. The exam tests record types, recursion vs iteration, TTL behavior, and how DNSSEC works.

flashcards.front: What do A, AAAA, CNAME, and MX records do?
flashcards.back: A: name → IPv4 address. AAAA: name → IPv6 address. CNAME: name → another name (an alias; cannot coexist with other records at the same name). MX: name → mail server with priority. TXT: arbitrary key-value (SPF, DKIM, domain ownership proofs). Memorize at least these five.

flashcards.front: Recursive vs authoritative resolver — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Authoritative: the server that owns the zone — when you ask 'what's the A record for example.com?' it answers definitively. Recursive: the client-side resolver (your ISP's, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) that walks the DNS hierarchy on your behalf, asking root → TLD → authoritative. Your laptop talks to a recursive resolver; the resolver talks to authoritatives.

Tells caching resolvers how long to keep a record. Low TTL (60s) = fast failover when you change records, but more DNS queries. High TTL (24h) = fewer queries, but a config change takes a day to propagate. Drop TTL to 60s a few hours BEFORE a planned migration; restore high TTL after.

flashcards.front: DNSSEC — what attack does it prevent?
flashcards.back: Cache poisoning: attacker injects fake records into a recursive resolver. DNSSEC signs records with the zone's private key; resolvers validate the signature against the DNS-published public key. If the signature doesn't match, the record is rejected. Adds CPU and complexity; most resolvers still don't strictly validate, but it's slowly winning.

questions.q: An architect needs to design a backup strategy for 200 Azure VMs across 5 subscriptions, ensuring all VMs are backed up daily with 30-day retention. A central team must be able to monitor backup compliance from a single dashboard. What is the recommended design?
choices: Deploy a third-party backup solution from the Azure Marketplace supporting multi-subscription daily backup with 30-day retention — adds licensing cost and lacks native Azure Policy enforcement and Backup Center dashboard
Create a Recovery Services Vault in each subscription and configure individual VM backup policies with daily frequency and 30-day retention

Enable Azure Snapshot Manager in Azure Monitor to schedule managed-disk daily snapshots with 30-day retention across subscriptions — disk snapshots only; not a full VM backup solution with policy-driven compliance monitoring
Use Azure Backup Center with an Azure Policy assignment that enforces a daily backup policy and 30-day retention across all 200 VMs in the 5 subscriptions from a single management pane
questions.explanation: Azure Backup Center is the unified management portal for all Azure Backup workloads across subscriptions, regions, and vault types. Combined with Azure Policy (built-in 'Configure backup on VMs with a given tag' policy), you can automatically enroll new VMs into backup, enforce retention policies, and monitor compliance status from a single pane. Recovery Services Vaults are still per-region/subscription but managed centrally. Backup Center provides cross-subscription reporting, compliance, and job monitoring dashboards.

questions.q: A company is designing its Azure storage strategy. Large files (video content, 50-500 GB each) will be uploaded once and accessed frequently for the first 30 days, rarely for the next 60 days, then almost never after 90 days. What lifecycle management policy minimizes cost?
choices: Store all files in the Hot tier permanently for 365 days or more, incurring maximum storage cost indefinitely instead of tiering to reduce cost over time
Store the videos in Premium block blob for fastest initial access for the first 30 days — highest cost tier with no automatic tiering to reduce cost after the hot-access window

Use Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 with auto-tiering enabled on the container — ADLS Gen2 does not natively support lifecycle management policies to minimise cost across the 30-day, 90-day, and 365-day access windows

Configure a Blob lifecycle management policy that transitions blobs to Cool at 30 days and to Archive at 365 days based on last-modified date — automated, zero-management tier transitions with cost optimisation
questions.explanation: Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management policies automate tier transitions based on last-modified time. The cost tiers (Hot > Cool > Cold > Archive) allow optimizing cost vs access latency. For this pattern: Hot (30 days, frequent access), Cool (30-90 days, infrequent), Archive (90+ days, near-zero access). Archive is the cheapest tier (~$0.00099/GB/month) but has rehydration latency (hours). Lifecycle policies run daily and transition blobs automatically, eliminating manual operations.

questions.q: A company requires a relational database solution that supports elastic scaling of compute independently of storage, can pause compute when not in use (dev/test scenarios), and provides per-second billing. Which Azure SQL offering fits?
choices: Azure SQL Database Serverless compute tier with auto-pause on inactivity, auto-resume on connection, and per-second compute billing — ideal for sporadic workloads

Azure SQL Database Hyperscale tier — elastic, distributed storage with rapid scale-out, but compute is always running with no auto-pause capability; per-second savings on idle periods are not available
Azure SQL Managed Instance General Purpose tier — managed instance with reserved vCore billing; compute runs continuously with no auto-pause on inactivity and no per-second idle billing reduction
Azure SQL Database Business Critical tier — highest performance with in-memory replica compute that is always on; no auto-pause or per-second cost reduction during inactivity-based suspension
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Database Serverless is purpose-built for intermittent, unpredictable usage patterns. It auto-scales compute vCores between a configured min and max based on workload, auto-pauses after a configurable inactivity period (minimum 60 minutes), and auto-resumes when a connection arrives (with a brief cold-start delay). Billing is per-second for active compute, plus per-GB for storage. This makes it ideal for dev/test databases that are idle nights and weekends. Business Critical and Managed Instance don't support auto-pause.

questions.q: An architect needs to choose a NoSQL database for a global e-commerce application that processes 1 million product catalog reads per second with single-digit millisecond latency. The data model is simple key-value lookups on product ID. Which Azure database service is most appropriate?
choices: Azure Table Storage — simple NoSQL key-value store at lower cost but without global active-active writes or guaranteed single-digit millisecond latency
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL with multi-region writes, autoscale RU/s, and a single-digit millisecond P99 read SLA
Azure SQL Database Business Critical tier with In-Memory OLTP tables — sub-millisecond in-region latency for transactions but not a single-digit millisecond globally distributed NoSQL solution
Azure Cache for Redis Premium as the primary catalog store with write-through replication — in-memory millisecond reads but not a durable globally distributed store with single-digit ms write latency
questions.explanation: Azure Cosmos DB is designed for planet-scale NoSQL with: single-digit millisecond read/write latency at the 99th percentile, automatic multi-region distribution with configurable consistency levels, elastic throughput scaling (Request Units, auto-scale), and 99.999% SLA for multi-region deployments. For 1M reads/second globally, Cosmos DB handles this natively. Azure Table Storage shares the Cosmos DB Table API but has lower SLAs and feature constraints. Redis is an in-memory cache (not a primary database). SQL with in-memory OLTP is still relational and has scaling limits.

questions.q: A retail company needs to ingest 50,000 IoT device events per second from sensors, transform the data, and load it into Azure Synapse Analytics for business intelligence reporting every 15 minutes. Which data pipeline architecture is appropriate?
choices: Azure IoT Hub → Stream Analytics with tumbling-window transforms → ADLS Gen2 landing zone → Synapse pipelines for BI
Azure Event Hubs → Azure Functions for event-by-event processing → Cosmos DB → Azure Synapse analytics queries — Functions processing is not optimised for streaming window analytics at IoT scale
Azure Event Grid → Azure Blob Storage → Azure Data Factory copy activity for periodic batch analytics loads — batch-oriented, not a streaming analytics pipeline with real-time transforms
Azure IoT Hub → Azure Logic Apps for transformation → Azure SQL Database → Power BI DirectQuery analytics — Logic Apps are low-throughput; not designed for high-volume streaming analytics
questions.explanation: The standard IoT analytics pattern on Azure: IoT Hub ingests device telemetry at scale (supports millions of devices), Stream Analytics provides real-time SQL-like transformations and windowing functions, ADLS Gen2 acts as the data lake landing zone, and Synapse Analytics pipelines (or Synapse Link) enable BI workloads. Stream Analytics supports 50K events/second and outputs to ADLS with time-based tumbling windows (15 min = perfect match). Logic Apps are for orchestration, not high-throughput stream processing. Event Grid is for event routing, not stream processing.

questions.q: A company wants to run batch machine learning training jobs that require thousands of CPU cores for 4-hour windows, twice a week. After the jobs complete, no compute should be running. What Azure compute solution minimizes cost?
choices: Azure Machine Learning compute clusters configured with min nodes = 0 and max nodes set to thousands — designed for ML training batch workloads, not general rendering batch pools with Spot VM auto-scale formulas
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets with scheduled autoscale rule scaling instance count
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) with the cluster autoscaler — container orchestration adds overhead not suited to ad-hoc rendering batch jobs that require Spot VM pools and auto-scale formulas
Azure Batch pools with auto-scale formulas and Spot/low-priority VMs to provision and tear down nodes per HPC job
questions.explanation: Azure Batch is specifically designed for large-scale parallel and HPC batch workloads. It manages pools of VMs, job scheduling, task distribution, and automatic scale-to-zero when idle. You only pay for VMs while they're running the batch job. Batch supports spot/low-priority VMs (60-90% discount) for further cost reduction. AML compute clusters also work but add ML-specific overhead. VMSS with scheduled scaling requires management. AKS adds Kubernetes overhead inappropriate for simple HPC batch workloads.

questions.q: An architect needs to host a containerized microservices application with 20 services. Some services need to scale to hundreds of instances under load, while others run 1-2 instances constantly. The team wants minimal Kubernetes management overhead. What is the recommended compute platform?
choices: Azure Container Instances (ACI) hosting all 20 services as serverless containers
Azure Functions on a consumption plan for all 20 microservices — minimal operational overhead for the team but not suited for long-running stateful services or Kubernetes-native workloads
Azure App Service Premium plans for every service with built-in autoscaling — reduces infrastructure overhead for the team but lacks Kubernetes native tooling, KEDA event-driven scaling, and HPA
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) with HPA and KEDA for per-service scaling, plus a managed control plane that absorbs the Kubernetes operational overhead for the team
questions.explanation: AKS is the recommended platform for containerized microservices requiring mixed scaling patterns. AKS manages the Kubernetes control plane (Azure pays for masters), leaving only node pool management. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling) enables scale-to-zero for idle services. The cluster autoscaler handles node-level scaling. Services needing hundreds of instances use Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) with appropriate resource requests. ACI is for simple on-demand containers, not long-running microservices. App Service doesn't support container orchestration at this complexity.

questions.q: A company is migrating a monolithic .NET Framework 4.8 application to Azure. The application cannot be refactored and requires full IIS control, custom GAC assemblies, and Windows Registry access. Which compute option is appropriate?
choices: Azure Container Instances running a Windows Server Core container image — provides near-full Windows compatibility but GAC registration and COM+ components are not supported in containerized IIS
Azure App Service (Windows) — managed PaaS with hosted IIS but without full Registry write access or GAC manipulation; global assemblies and COM+ components are unsupported
Azure Virtual Machines running Windows Server with full IIS, GAC, and Registry access for the legacy .NET Framework 4.8 monolith
Azure Functions on the .NET Framework in-process runtime — lightweight but without full IIS hosting model, GAC access, or COM+ component support for complex legacy dependencies
questions.explanation: When an application requires deep OS-level customization (Windows Registry, GAC, specific IIS module configuration, COM+ components), a Virtual Machine (IaaS) is the appropriate lift-and-shift target. Azure App Service has Windows IIS support but restricts Registry and GAC access. Azure Functions requires refactoring to serverless. Windows containers support GAC but not all Registry paths and COM+ scenarios. The AZ-305 approach: migrate first to IaaS (full compatibility), then modernize to PaaS progressively if feasible.

correct.useCase: The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after an outage — it drives your BCDR design choices.

distractors.useCase: A policy setting that enforces tags on new resources.
Routes users to the lowest-latency Azure region.
Moves an RBAC assignment between users.

nodes.title: Azure API Management (AZ-204 / AZ-305): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Azure API Management (APIM) is a managed gateway layer that sits in front of backend APIs. AZ-204 tests the four policy sections (inbound, backend, outbound, on-error) that transform and govern requests, the rate-limiting and JWT-validation policies, response caching, and the developer portal for external API consumers.

flashcards.front: APIM policy sections — what runs in each of the four phases?
flashcards.back: Inbound: runs first on the request before it reaches the backend — authentication (validate-jwt), rate limiting (rate-limit-by-key), request transformation (set-header, rewrite-uri), IP filtering. Backend: controls how the gateway calls the backend — retry policy, circuit breaker, load balancing between backends. Outbound: transforms the response before returning to the caller — add/remove headers, mask sensitive fields, inject CORS headers. On-error: handles exceptions — return custom error responses, log diagnostics.

flashcards.front: rate-limit-by-key policy — how does it work?
flashcards.back: Limits the number of calls per key (subscription, IP, JWT claim) within a time window. Example: `<rate-limit-by-key calls="100" renewal-period="60" counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" />` limits each subscriber to 100 calls per 60 seconds. Returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header when exceeded. Use `quota-by-key` for soft monthly caps (reset monthly, not per second). These are the primary monetization / abuse-prevention levers in APIM.

flashcards.front: validate-jwt policy — what does it verify?
flashcards.back: Validates a Bearer JWT in the Authorization header (or a custom header/query param). Checks signature against a specified JWKS URI or symmetric key, verifies iss (issuer), aud (audience), exp (expiry), and nbf (not before). Can also require specific claims to be present. On failure, returns HTTP 401 without forwarding to the backend. This centralizes auth at the gateway so individual backends don't need to implement JWT validation.

flashcards.front: APIM developer portal — what is it for?
flashcards.back: An auto-generated, customizable website where external developers discover, read documentation for, and subscribe to your APIs. It shows OpenAPI specs rendered as interactive try-it-out pages, subscription key management, and usage analytics. Consumers sign up, get an API key (subscription key), and test calls from the portal. It separates the developer onboarding experience from the API implementation — a standard requirement for public or partner APIs.

questions.q: An e-commerce application experiences Black Friday spikes of 100x normal traffic. The application is hosted on Azure App Service. The architect wants the application to scale out automatically based on HTTP request queue length, not just CPU. Which autoscaling approach enables custom metric scaling?
choices: Azure App Service automatic scaling (preview) based on average HTTP request latency metric — uses latency-based triggers to scale but does not target queue depth which better represents backend saturation
Configure App Service autoscale rules on the HttpQueueLength metric — scale out when > 10, scale in when < 1

Use Azure Traffic Manager to distribute traffic across multiple App Service plans when load increases — DNS-based traffic routing, not a solution to scale out compute within a single App Service plan based on queue depth

Deploy Azure Front Door with origin groups to absorb traffic spikes at the edge tier before they reach the backend — edge caching and routing, not a mechanism to scale App Service compute based on HttpQueueLength
questions.explanation: Azure App Service exposes custom metrics including HttpQueueLength (number of requests waiting in the HTTP queue) that can trigger autoscale rules. This metric is more relevant for queue-based bottlenecks than CPU — a healthy app might have low CPU but a growing HTTP queue if I/O-bound. Autoscale rules: scale out when HttpQueueLength > 10 (add instances), scale in when < 1 (remove instances). This provides more responsive scaling than CPU for web workloads. Traffic Manager is DNS-level, not application-level autoscaling.

questions.q: A solutions architect needs to design an API layer for a microservices application. The API must support rate limiting, request/response transformation, authentication (JWT validation), developer portal for API documentation, and monetization through subscription keys. Which Azure service provides all of these capabilities?
choices: Azure API Management — provides inbound/outbound policies for rate limiting and transformation, JWT validation, a developer portal for API subscription and key management, and monetisation tiers

Azure Application Gateway with WAF SKU — provides Layer-7 load balancing and WAF protection for the developer portal but lacks native API transformation policies, subscription key management, or SOAP-to-REST conversion

Azure Functions with custom middleware — can implement rate limiting and JWT validation in code but requires building the developer portal, subscription key management, and transformation logic from scratch

Azure Front Door with Rules Engine — provides global edge routing and WAF but lacks native API transformation policies, subscription key management, and a built-in developer portal for API monetisation
questions.explanation: Azure API Management is specifically designed as a full-lifecycle API management platform. Key features: Inbound/outbound policies (rate limiting, IP filtering, JWT validation, header transformation), OAuth2/OpenID Connect integration, developer portal (auto-generated API documentation, subscription management), product tiers with subscription keys for monetization, built-in analytics, and backend load balancing. Application Gateway and Front Door are network-layer load balancers without API management capabilities. Azure Functions require building all cross-cutting concerns from scratch.

questions.q: An architect is designing a solution for an application that processes financial transactions. Each transaction must be processed exactly once, in order, and failures must be retried without duplicate processing. Which messaging pattern is most appropriate?
choices: Azure Event Hubs for real-time transaction streaming with multiple consumer groups — high-throughput but no built-in FIFO ordering or duplicate detection for exactly-once financial transactions
Azure Storage Queue with at-least-once delivery and application-level duplicate detection
Azure Service Bus Queues with message sessions for FIFO ordering per session key, plus duplicate detection enabled to automatically discard re-submitted transactions
Azure Event Grid for event-driven transaction processing with built-in retry policies — push-based, no FIFO sessions, not designed for ordered exactly-once financial transactions processing
questions.explanation: Service Bus Queues provide exactly-once, ordered processing through: (1) Message Sessions — enables FIFO ordering per session key (e.g., account ID), ensuring transactions for the same account are processed in order, (2) Duplicate detection — if a message is resent with the same MessageId within a configurable window, Service Bus discards the duplicate, (3) Dead-letter queue (DLQ) for messages that fail after max retries. Event Hubs is optimized for high-throughput telemetry streaming, not reliable ordered business transactions. Storage Queue has no ordering guarantee and no duplicate detection.

questions.q: A developer team wants to deploy a web application using containers to Azure with no Kubernetes management overhead, automatic HTTPS, built-in scale-to-zero, and support for sidecar containers. Which Azure service provides all of these?
choices: Azure Container Apps — managed serverless container platform with KEDA autoscale including scale-to-zero on HTTPS traffic, Dapr sidecar support, and no Kubernetes management overhead
Azure Container Instances (ACI) — runs containers without a cluster or Kubernetes overhead, with per-second billing, but has no built-in HTTPS autoscaling, scale-to-zero triggers, or sidecar support
Azure App Service for Containers — managed PaaS with HTTPS autoscale and no Kubernetes management, but limited to single-container workloads without KEDA or Dapr sidecar support

Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) with Virtual Nodes — provides KEDA scale-to-zero and full Kubernetes sidecar support but requires managing the Kubernetes control plane, cluster upgrades, and node configurations
questions.explanation: Azure Container Apps is the modern PaaS for microservices containers without Kubernetes management. It provides: KEDA-based autoscaling including scale-to-zero, built-in HTTPS ingress with auto-managed TLS certificates, sidecar container support (Dapr integration), revision management for blue-green deployments, and support for event-driven architectures. ACI is for single containers without built-in HTTP ingress or KEDA scaling. App Service supports containers but doesn't support sidecars natively. AKS requires cluster management.

questions.q: A company processes 10 million Azure AD sign-in logs per day and needs to retain them for 90 days with the ability to query specific user sign-in events interactively. Log Analytics ingestion costs are a concern. Which cost-optimized design supports this?
choices: Ingest all 10M daily sign-in logs into the standard Log Analytics Analytics-plan table at the workspace's normal ingestion price
Use Microsoft Sentinel on the Log Analytics workspace with a commitment tier purchased to obtain a volume ingestion discount
Archive the sign-in logs to Azure Storage cool tier and query them with a self-hosted ELK stack running on Azure VMs
Send the sign-in logs via Diagnostic Settings to a Log Analytics workspace using the Basic logs table for cheaper ingestion
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor Logs introduced Basic and Auxiliary log plans (alongside the standard Analytics plan). Basic plan: significantly lower ingestion cost (~$0.50/GB vs ~$2.30/GB for Analytics), 8-day interactive query retention, archival for up to 12 years. For Azure AD Sign-In Logs where you primarily need to search specific events (not complex analytics), the Basic plan delivers significant cost savings. Analytics plan provides full KQL capabilities but at higher cost. The AZ-305 cost optimization domain tests knowledge of log plan tiers.

questions.q: An organization must implement multi-region active-active deployment for a web application with shared state. Users must always be routed to the nearest healthy region, and sessions must be consistent across regions. Which Azure services form this architecture?
choices: Azure Traffic Manager with Geographic routing plus Azure SQL Database Active Geo-Replication — routes to the nearest healthy region via DNS but supports only one active primary; Active Geo-Replication is active-passive, not a multi-region shared state active-active architecture

Azure Front Door for global traffic routing with health probes plus Azure Cosmos DB with multi-region writes — both components are designed for active-active; Front Door routes to the nearest healthy origin; Cosmos DB handles multi-region shared state
Azure Load Balancer Standard cross-region plus Azure Cache for Redis Premium geo-replication

Azure Application Gateway in each region behind Traffic Manager DNS plus Azure SQL Database with auto-failover — Application Gateway is regional L7 only; SQL auto-failover is active-passive shared state, not a nearest-healthy active-active solution
questions.explanation: Azure Front Door provides global anycast routing to the nearest healthy region with sub-second health probe detection and automatic failover. For active-active with shared session state, Cosmos DB with multi-region write (also called multi-master) is the key: any region can write sessions, with automatic conflict resolution and replication to all regions. SQL Geo-Replication provides read-only secondaries — cannot write to secondaries in active-active. Redis geo-replication is asynchronous and doesn't support multi-master writes.

questions.q: A company's security team requires that all access to Azure Key Vault secrets from application VMs happens over private network paths — no public internet. The VMs are in an Azure VNet. Which network design achieves this?
choices: Enable the Key Vault firewall and add the VNet subnet to the allowed Virtual Networks list — restricts access but still uses the public Key Vault internet endpoint; traffic leaves the private VNet to reach the public-facing URL

Deploy Azure Firewall in the hub VNet and add the Key Vault FQDN to its allowed application rules — routes traffic through the firewall but does not eliminate the public internet endpoint; Key Vault is still reached via its private DNS or public endpoint
Configure NSG outbound rules on the application subnet to block all egress except traffic to the Key Vault public IP
Deploy a Private Endpoint for the Key Vault in the application VNet with a Private DNS Zone so all Key Vault traffic stays on the private network without traversing the public internet
questions.explanation: Private Endpoints create a private network interface with a private IP address within your VNet for the Key Vault. Azure Private DNS Zones override public DNS resolution so 'vault.vault.azure.net' resolves to the private IP instead of the public endpoint. All traffic from VMs to Key Vault flows through the VNet/backbone, never traversing the internet. Service Endpoints keep traffic on the backbone but the Key Vault endpoint is still a public IP from the VM's perspective — it doesn't provide full private connectivity for all scenarios. Private Endpoint is the recommended approach for strict private access requirements.

questions.q: A startup is designing its first Azure application — a web app with a REST API backend and a SQL database. The team has 2 developers and needs to be productive with minimal infrastructure management. The expected load is 100-500 users/day for the first 6 months. What is the most appropriate architecture?
choices: Azure App Service Basic tier for the web app and API, Azure SQL Database S0 DTU tier, and Application Insights for monitoring
Azure Kubernetes Service with a managed node pool, an Ingress controller, and Azure SQL Database General Purpose backing it
Azure Virtual Machines for the API (Windows Server + IIS), Azure SQL Database Basic tier, and Azure Application Gateway in front
Azure Functions consumption plan for the API, Cosmos DB serverless for data, and Azure Static Web Apps for the frontend
questions.explanation: For a small team with minimal operations overhead and low initial load, PaaS services are ideal: App Service manages OS patching, scaling, and TLS; Azure SQL Database manages backup, patching, and HA. The Basic/Standard DTU tiers are cost-effective for 100-500 users/day. Application Insights provides out-of-the-box APM. This is the AZ-305 principle of 'right-sizing and right-tiering' — AKS is over-engineered for a 2-person startup. VMs add infrastructure management burden. Functions/Cosmos DB works but adds complexity when the team may not need it yet.

nodes.title: Role-based access control: Key Ideas
nodes.content: RBAC assigns permissions to roles, then users to roles — a layer of indirection that scales. Azure's RBAC, AWS's IAM, Kubernetes RBAC, and GCP's IAM all share the same mental model. Mastering one transfers directly to the others.

flashcards.front: Why use roles instead of granting permissions to users directly?
flashcards.back: Roles separate WHO from WHAT. Add a person to a role, they inherit the permissions. Remove them, they lose access instantly. Auditing: 'who can read prod?' becomes 'who's in the prod-readers role?' instead of scanning thousands of user-level policies. Onboarding/offboarding becomes role membership changes, not 500 permission grants.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between a built-in role and a custom role?
flashcards.back: Built-in: cloud-provided, covers common patterns (Owner, Contributor, Reader, Storage Admin). Can't be modified. Custom: you define the exact actions allowed — pick when built-ins are too broad or too narrow. Cost of custom roles: maintenance — every new service adds actions you may need to add.

flashcards.front: Scope — why is it as important as the role?
flashcards.back: Same role at different scopes = wildly different power. 'Contributor' at the subscription scope = god mode on the whole subscription. 'Contributor' on one resource group = limited to that group's resources. Always scope at the smallest unit that's practical — never grant subscription-level if resource-group-level works.

flashcards.front: RBAC vs ABAC — when do you need attributes?
flashcards.back: RBAC: permissions tied to fixed roles. Works great until you need rules like 'engineers can read their own team's resources but not others'. ABAC (attribute-based) evaluates request attributes (user.team, resource.team) at runtime. Most clouds support both — start with RBAC, add ABAC tags when the role explosion becomes painful.

questions.q: A company's compliance team requires that ALL changes to Azure resources (creates, updates, deletes) in their production subscription be logged and retained for 1 year. The logs must be queryable. What is the correct configuration?
choices: Configure a Diagnostic Setting at the subscription scope exporting Activity Logs to a Log Analytics workspace with 365-day retention

Deploy Microsoft Sentinel and connect the Azure Activity data connector — Sentinel ingests activity logs for security analytics but does not provide a simple subscription-scoped diagnostic setting for 90-day logs retention

Enable Azure Policy with 'Audit if Activity Log is not retained' built-in initiative — audits the absence of logs retention settings but does not configure the diagnostic setting itself to export activity logs

Enable Defender for Cloud on the subscription — security posture tool that surfaces activity-related alerts but does not configure a subscription-level diagnostic setting to retain activity logs for 90 days
questions.explanation: Azure Activity Logs capture all control-plane operations (resource creates, updates, deletes, RBAC changes, policy assignments) for the subscription. By default they're retained 90 days. To retain for 1 year: create a Diagnostic Setting at the subscription scope to export Activity Logs to a Log Analytics workspace (configure 365-day retention) or Azure Storage. The workspace enables KQL querying. This is standard configuration — no additional services like Defender or Sentinel are required, though they may augment it.

questions.q: An architect needs to design a solution where an Azure Function needs to call multiple Azure services (Blob Storage, Cosmos DB, Key Vault) without storing any credentials or connection strings in the function's application settings. Which identity pattern is recommended?
choices: Store the credentials encrypted in Azure Key Vault and configure the Function to fetch them at startup — requires an identity to authenticate to Key Vault; does not eliminate credentials by using managed identity natively
Enable system-assigned Managed Identity on the Function and grant it the appropriate data-plane RBAC role on each target service

Create a service principal in Azure AD with certificates stored in Key Vault and use it for authentication — service principal requires managing certificate rotation, unlike a managed identity with automatic credential lifecycle

Store all connection strings in Azure App Configuration with access-key authentication — access keys are static credentials, not a managed identity approach; does not eliminate the secret from application configuration
questions.explanation: Managed Identity eliminates credential management entirely — there are no secrets to store, rotate, or secure. The system-assigned MI is automatically created and bound to the Function lifecycle. Azure services that support Azure AD authentication (Blob Storage, Cosmos DB, Key Vault, Service Bus, Event Hubs, SQL Database) can authenticate the managed identity via RBAC or access policies. This is the #1 AZ-305 recommended pattern for Azure-to-Azure service authentication. Key Vault references (option D) still require an authentication credential for Key Vault itself.

questions.q: A company wants to build a serverless event-driven architecture where order placement events trigger inventory updates, billing, and notification workflows independently. If one downstream service is temporarily unavailable, the event must be retried without losing it. Which Azure messaging service is designed for this pattern?
choices: Azure Event Grid — serverless event routing with at-least-once delivery, exponential retry, and dead-lettering per subscriber
Azure Storage Queue — simple queuing with at-least-once delivery for background job processing; not a serverless event routing service with push delivery and exponential retry policies
Azure Service Bus — reliable message queuing with competing consumers and ordered processing; requires always-on consumers and is not a serverless event router with native push-based event delivery

Azure Event Hubs — high-throughput streaming for real-time analytics on order events; not a serverless event router, requires consumer groups polling continuously rather than push-based serverless delivery
questions.explanation: Azure Event Grid is purpose-built for event-driven pub/sub scenarios: publishers emit events (Order Placed), and multiple subscribers (inventory service, billing service, notification service) receive independent copies. Event Grid provides at-least-once delivery with built-in retry (exponential backoff, up to 24 hours), dead-lettering for undeliverable events, and subscriber isolation (one subscriber's failure doesn't affect others). Service Bus is for reliable ordered queue-based messaging (point-to-point or pub/sub with sessions). Event Hubs is for high-throughput telemetry streaming with consumer groups.

questions.q: A company needs to deploy a highly available web application in Azure with connection-based session affinity (sticky sessions) and SSL offloading. The web tier has 10 VMs in the same VNet. Which load balancer supports these requirements?
choices: Azure Front Door — global anycast application delivery with SSL offloading and session affinity applied at the edge POPs
Azure Traffic Manager — DNS-based global load balancer with the Subnet routing method providing endpoint-affinity
Azure Load Balancer Standard — layer 4 load balancing with health probes but no SSL termination or cookie affinity
Azure Application Gateway — layer 7 load balancer with cookie-based session affinity, SSL offloading, and optional WAF
questions.explanation: Azure Application Gateway is a layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) load balancer. Key features for this scenario: Cookie-based affinity inserts a custom cookie on the first response, binding the client to a specific backend for subsequent requests (sticky sessions). SSL/TLS offloading terminates HTTPS at the gateway, allowing HTTP communication to backends (reducing backend CPU load). WAF can be added for web application protection. ALB Standard is layer 4 — it can do hash-based affinity (source IP) but not cookie-based, and doesn't terminate SSL. Traffic Manager is DNS-level (no sticky sessions within a region).

questions.q: An architect needs to design an Azure solution for running a legacy application that requires a Windows Server 2012 R2 environment. The company policy mandates that all Azure VMs must use the latest security updates. How should the patching strategy be designed?
choices: Manual patching performed by the system administrators via RDP on each VM during a monthly maintenance window
Azure Update Manager (formerly Update Management Center) for centralized patch assessment and scheduled deployments
Azure Automation Hybrid Runbook Worker running custom patch scripts on each VM via PowerShell DSC compliance
Azure Guest OS automatic patching enabled on the VMs so Azure applies all available patches without explicit scheduling
questions.explanation: Azure Update Manager provides centralized patch management for Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers. It assesses missing patches in real-time without deploying a management solution, creates patching schedules with maintenance windows to minimize disruption, supports reboot preferences, pre/post maintenance scripts, and cross-subscription multi-VM management from a single view. It supports Windows Server 2012 R2 through current versions. Guest OS automatic patching is limited to Azure-recommended patches and has limited schedule control — not suitable for controlled production environments.

questions.q: A company needs a storage solution for SMB file shares that Windows VMs access like traditional on-premises network drives. The solution must support Active Directory authentication for access control and provide 99.99% availability SLA. Which Azure service provides this?
choices: Azure NetApp Files for enterprise NFS and SMB workloads with three performance tiers — high availability storage but does not natively support AD DS authentication for Windows SMB file shares with ZRS-backed availability
Azure Disk Storage in shared-disk configuration backing a clustered Windows Server File Server
Azure Files Premium with the SMB 3.0 protocol, AD DS authentication, and ZRS for the 99.99% availability SLA

Azure Blob Storage with the NFS v3 protocol enabled for Windows VM access via the NFS client — NFS v3 on Blob Storage does not support SMB 3.0 or AD DS authentication for Windows-native file share availability
questions.explanation: Azure Files provides fully managed SMB file shares in Azure. Premium tier with ZRS (Zone-Redundant Storage) provides 99.99% SLA. Azure AD Kerberos authentication (or on-premises AD DS integration) allows existing AD users/groups to access shares with their domain credentials — no separate user management. Windows VMs mount the share as a network drive using standard UNC paths. This is the recommended migration target for on-premises file servers. NetApp Files is for high-performance NFS/SMB but at significantly higher cost. Blob NFS is for Linux POSIX workloads.

questions.q: A solutions architect needs to design a globally distributed application that caches frequently read data to minimize database load. The cache must be highly available within a region and should share no single point of failure between cache and primary database. Which Azure caching solution supports replication within a region for HA?
choices: Azure Cosmos DB integrated cache configured in front of the container for sub-millisecond reads

Azure Content Delivery Network for caching API responses at edge POPs globally with origin shield — edge HTTP response caching; no primary-replica replication, persistence, or automatic failover for in-memory cache data

Azure Table Storage with row-level caching enabled for frequently accessed records — Azure Table Storage has no row-level caching feature; not a primary-replica in-memory cache with automatic failover
Azure Cache for Redis Standard or Premium tier with primary-replica replication, automatic failover, and a 99.9%+ SLA
questions.explanation: Azure Cache for Redis is the managed in-memory data store for caching, session storage, and message brokering. Standard tier provides a two-node primary-replica setup with automatic failover and 99.9% SLA. Premium tier adds clustering (multiple shards), persistence (RDB/AOF), and geo-replication for cross-region cache reads. This directly addresses the HA requirement within a region. CDN caches static content at edge, not application-layer cache. Table Storage is a persistent database, not a cache. Cosmos DB integrated cache is a feature for Cosmos DB itself, not a general-purpose caching layer.

questions.q: An architect is designing a network solution that requires Azure VMs in one VNet to communicate with services in a third-party SaaS provider's Azure VNet, without exposing traffic to the internet and without requiring VNet peering. What technology enables this?
choices: Use Azure ExpressRoute Microsoft Peering to route traffic between the two VNets through the Microsoft global backbone
Deploy a Site-to-Site IPsec VPN tunnel between the company's VNet gateway and the SaaS provider's VNet gateway
Configure VNet peering directly between the company's VNet and the SaaS provider's VNet across the two tenants
The SaaS provider publishes a Private Link Service and the consumer creates a Private Endpoint in its own VNet
questions.explanation: Azure Private Link enables service providers to expose their services as Private Link Services. Consumers create a Private Endpoint in their own VNet, which receives a private IP in the consumer's address space. Traffic flows from the consumer VM → consumer VNet → Azure backbone → Private Link Service → provider VNet without VNet peering (no overlapping IP concerns), without internet exposure, and without the provider needing visibility into the consumer's network. This is the standard pattern for SaaS providers (including Microsoft PaaS services) and enterprise service sharing.
